claims.text: [penalty_summary] This Decision establishes no fine, penalty, or sanction regime: it is a consistency finding confirming that Poland's draft RP3 performance targets align with the Union-wide targets, with no enforcement provision of its own.

[primary_deadline] The recitals record that all Member States' draft RP3 performance plans, including Poland's, were submitted to the Commission for assessment by 1 October 2021 -- background context for this consistency finding, not a forward deadline imposed by this Decision's own operative Articles.

claims.text: [jurisdictional_scope] This Decision is addressed to the Republic of Poland (assessing the draft performance plan Poland submitted pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 549/2004).
claims.span: This Decision is addressed to the Republic of Poland.

claims.text: [effective_date] This Decision contains no entry-into-force clause: its two Articles record a consistency finding and name the addressee, with no separate date stated for when the Decision itself takes effect beyond the adoption date of 13 April 2022 recorded in the preamble.

Article 1: The performance targets contained in the draft performance plan submitted by Poland, pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 549/2004, and listed in the Annex to this Decision, are consistent with the Union-wide performance targets for the third reference period set out in Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/891.

Article 2: This Decision is addressed to the Republic of Poland.

pool.text: 18.5.2022 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 139/208 COMMISSION DECISION (EU) 2022/779 of 13 April 2022 on the consistency of the performance targets contained in the draft performance plan submitted by Poland pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 549/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council with the Union-wide performance targets for the third reference period (notified under document C(2022) 2304) (Only the Polish text is authentic) (Text with EEA relevance) THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION, Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Having regard to Regulation (EC) No 549/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 March 2004 laying down the framework for the creation of the single European sky (the framework Regulation) (1), and in particular Article 11(3) point (c), first paragraph, thereof, Having regard to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317 of 11 February 2019 laying down a performance and charging scheme in the single European sky (2), and in particular Article 14(2) thereof, Whereas: GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS (1) Pursuant to Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 549/2004, a performance scheme for air navigation services and network functions is to be set up. Furthermore, pursuant to Article 10 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, Member States are to draw up, either at national level or at the level of functional airspace blocks (‘FABs’), binding performance targets for each reference period of the performance scheme for air navigation services and network functions. Those performance targets have to be consistent with the Union-wide targets adopted by the Commission for the reference period concerned. The Commission is responsible for assessing whether the proposed performance targets contained in the draft performance plans drawn up by the Member States are consistent with the Union-wide performance targets using the assessment criteria set out in Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. (2) The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic has, since the first quarter of calendar year 2020, significantly impacted the air transport sector and has considerably reduced air traffic volumes as compared to pre-pandemic levels, due to the measures taken by the Member States and third countries to contain the pandemic. (3) Union-wide performance targets for the third reference period (‘RP3’) were originally set out in Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2019/903 (3). As those Union-wide performance targets and the draft RP3 performance plans subsequently submitted by the Member States were drawn up before the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, they could not take account of the resulting significantly changed circumstances for air transport. (4) In response to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the provision of air navigation services, exceptional measures for RP3, which derogate from the provisions of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, were set out in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1627 (4). Pursuant to Article 2(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1627, the Commission adopted, on 2 June 2021, Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/891 (5) setting revised Union-wide performance targets for RP3. (5) The Commission notes that the October 2021 base traffic forecast of the Eurocontrol’s Statistics and Forecast Service (‘STATFOR’) projects that air traffic at Union-wide level will reach its pre-pandemic levels in the course of 2023 and will exceed those levels in 2024. However, the level of uncertainty regarding traffic development remains particularly high because of the risks related to the evolution of the COVID-19 epidemiological situation. The Commission also notes that the traffic recovery is expected to be uneven across Member States. (6) All Member States have developed and adopted draft performance plans containing revised local performance targets for RP3, which were submitted to the Commission for assessment by 1 October 2021. Following the verification of completeness of those draft performance plans, the Commission requested Member States to submit updated draft performance plans by 17 November 2021. The Commission’s assessment presented in this Decision is based on the updated draft performance plan submitted by Poland. (7) The performance review body, assisting the Commission in the implementation of the performance scheme pursuant to Article 11(2) of Regulation (EC) No 549/2004, has submitted to the Commission a report containing its advice on the assessment of RP3 draft performance plans. (8) In accordance with Article 14(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, the Commission has assessed the consistency of the local performance targets proposed by Poland on the basis of the assessment criteria laid down in point 1 of Annex IV to that Implementing Regulation, and taking account of local circumstances. In respect of each key performance area and the related performance targets, the Commission has complemented the assessment by reviewing draft performance plans in respect of the elements set out in point 2 of Annex IV to that Implementing Regulation. COMMISSION ASSESSMENT Assessment of draft performance targets in the key performance area of safety (9) Concerning the key performance area of safety, the Commission has assessed the consistency of the targets submitted by Poland regarding the effectiveness of safety management of air navigation service providers based on the criterion laid down in point 1.1 of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. That assessment was conducted taking account of local circumstances and was complemented by the review of measures planned for the achievement of the safety targets in respect of the elements set out in point 2.1.(a) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. (10) The draft performance targets in the key performance area of safety proposed by Poland in respect of the effectiveness of safety management, broken down per safety management objective and expressed as a level of implementation, are as follows: Poland Targets on the effectiveness of safety management, expressed as a level of implementation, ranging from EASA level A to D Air navigation service providers concerned Safety management objective 2021 2022 2023 2024 PANSA, Warmia i Mazury sp. z o.o., Port Lotniczy Bydgoszcz S.A. Safety policy and objectives C C C C Safety risk management C C C D Safety assurance C C C C Safety promotion C C C C Safety culture C C C C (11) In respect of the draft safety targets proposed by Poland for all the covered air navigation service providers, the Commission has found that the level of the Union-wide performance target is planned to be achieved in 2024 with regard to the ‘safety risk management’ objective, whilst for the other ‘safety management objectives’ the local performance targets meet the level of the Union-wide performance target for each calendar year from 2021 to 2024. (12) The Commission notes that the draft performance plan submitted by Poland sets out measures for the ANSPs for the achievement of the local safety targets, such as measures to ensure compliance with Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/373 (6), a review of safety processes, an update of safety trainings for managers, the development of safety management indicators, continued safety promotion, as well as the implementation of best practices, documents and procedures in line with national and international regulations. (13) On the basis of the findings set out in recitals 11 and 12, and considering that the Union-wide safety performance targets set in Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/891 must be achieved by the final year of RP3, namely 2024, the draft targets included in the draft performance plan of Poland should be assessed as consistent with the Union-wide performance targets in the key performance area of safety. Assessment of draft performance targets in the key performance area of environment (14) Concerning the key performance area of environment, the consistency of the targets submitted by Poland regarding the average horizontal en route flight efficiency of the actual trajectory has been assessed based on the criterion laid down in point 1.2 of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. Accordingly, the proposed targets contained in the draft performance plan of Poland have been compared to the relevant en route horizontal flight efficiency reference values set out in the European Route Network Improvement Plan (‘ERNIP’) available at the time of adopting the revised Union-wide performance targets for RP3, that is on 2 June 2021. That assessment was conducted taking account of local circumstances and was complemented by the review of measures planned for the achievement of the environment targets under point 2.1(a) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. (15) In respect of the calendar year 2020, the Union-wide performance target for RP3 in the key performance area of environment, which was initially set out in Implementing Decision (EU) 2019/903, was not revised by Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/891, considering that the time period for the application of that target had expired and that its implementation had thus become definitive leaving no possibility for retroactive adjustments. Accordingly, Member States were not requested to revise, in the draft performance plans submitted by 1 October 2021, their local performance targets for calendar year 2020 in the key performance area of environment. Therefore, the consistency of the local environment performance targets with the corresponding Union-wide performance targets should be assessed with regard to calendar years 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024. (16) The draft performance targets in the key performance area of environment proposed by Poland and the corresponding national reference values for RP3 from the ERNIP, expressed as the average horizontal en route flight efficiency of the actual trajectory, are as follows: 2021 2022 2023 2024 Draft en route environment targets of Poland, expressed as the average horizontal en route flight efficiency of the actual trajectory 1,65 % 1,65 % 1,65 % 1,65 % Reference values for Poland 1,65 % 1,65 % 1,65 % 1,65 % (17) The Commission observes that the draft environment targets proposed by Poland are equal to the corresponding national reference values for each calendar year from 2021 to 2024. (18) In respect of point 2.1(a) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, the Commission notes that Poland has presented in the draft performance plan several measures for the achievement of the local environment targets which include the reorganisation of sector configurations for the Warsaw Area Control Centre, implementation of advanced flexible use of airspace concepts as well as improvements in Warsaw Terminal Manoeuvring Area. (19) Furthermore, the Commission observes that Poland has already implemented free route airspace (FRA) between flight level 95 and flight level 660 since February 2019. The Commission also notes that Poland plans to further expand FRA with the Baltic FAB, Slovakia and Ukraine in calendar year 2024. (20) On the basis of the findings set out in recitals 17 to 19, the draft targets included in the draft performance plan of Poland should be assessed as consistent with the Union-wide performance targets in the key performance area of environment. Assessment of draft performance targets in the key performance area of capacity (21) Concerning the key performance area of capacity, the consistency of the targets submitted by Poland regarding the average en route air traffic flow management (‘ATFM’) delay per flight has been assessed based on the criterion laid down in point 1.3 of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. Accordingly, the proposed targets contained in the draft performance plan of Poland have been compared to the relevant reference values set out in the Network Operations Plan available at the time of adopting the revised Union-wide performance targets for RP3, that is on 2 June 2021. That assessment was conducted taking account of local circumstances and was complemented by the review of measures planned for the achievement of the capacity targets under point 2.1(a) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. (22) In respect of the calendar year 2020, the Union-wide performance target for RP3 in the key performance area of capacity, which was initially set out in Implementing Decision (EU) 2019/903, was not revised by Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/891, considering that the time period for the application of that target had expired and that its implementation had thus become definitive leaving no possibility for retroactive adjustments. Accordingly, Member States were not requested to revise, in the draft performance plans submitted by 1 October 2021, their local performance targets for calendar year 2020 in the key performance area of capacity. Therefore, the consistency of the local capacity performance targets with the corresponding Union-wide performance targets should be assessed with regard to calendar years 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024. (23) The draft en route capacity targets proposed by Poland for RP3, expressed in minutes of ATFM delay per flight, as well as the corresponding reference values from the Network Operations Plan are as follows: 2021 2022 2023 2024 Draft en route capacity targets of Poland, in minutes of ATFM delay per flight 0,07 0,12 0,12 0,12 Reference values for Poland 0,07 0,12 0,12 0,12 (24) The Commission observes that the draft capacity targets proposed by Poland are equal to the corresponding national reference values for each calendar year from 2021 to 2024. (25) In respect of point 2.1(a) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, the Commission notes that Poland has presented in the draft performance plan a range of measures for the achievement of the local en route capacity targets. Those measures include continued air traffic controller training, flexible staff planning and rostering, increased number of sectors and improved sector opening times as well as the implementation of cross-border FRA. (26) On the basis of the findings set out in recitals 24 and 25, the draft targets included in the draft performance plan of Poland should be assessed as consistent with the Union-wide performance targets in the key performance area of capacity. Review of draft capacity targets for terminal air navigation services (27) With regard to airports which fall within the scope of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317 as set out in Articles 1(3) and (4) of that Regulation, the Commission has complemented its assessment of draft en route capacity targets by the review of the draft capacity targets for terminal air navigation services in accordance with point 2.1(b) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. Those draft targets were found to raise concerns in respect of Poland. (28) Specifically, when comparing at airport level the draft national targets on average arrival ATFM delay with the performance of similar airports during the second reference period (‘RP2’), the Commission has found that the airports of Warszawa-Chopin, Warszawa-Modlin, Krakow-Balice and Katowice-Pyrzowice are expected to experience higher ATFM delays than those forecasted for similar airports. (29) Therefore, the Commission considers that, in connection with the adoption of its final performance plan in accordance with Article 16, point (a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, Poland should further justify the terminal capacity targets for RP3 in light of the observations set out in recital 28, or should revise downwards those targets. Assessment of draft performance targets in the key performance area of cost-efficiency (30) Concerning the key performance area of cost-efficiency, the consistency of the targets submitted by Poland regarding the determined unit costs (‘DUC’) for en route air navigation services has been assessed based on the criteria laid down in points 1.4(a), (b) and (c) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. Those criteria consist of the DUC trend over RP3, the long-term DUC trend over RP2 and RP3 (2015-2024), and the baseline value for the DUC at charging zone level compared with the average value of the charging zones where air navigation service providers have a similar operational and economic environment. (31) The assessment of en route cost efficiency targets was conducted taking account of local circumstances. It was complemented by the review of the key factors and parameters underpinning those targets as specified in point 2.1(d) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. (32) The draft en route cost-efficiency targets proposed by Poland for RP3 are as follows: En route charging zone of Poland 2014 baseline value 2019 baseline value 2020 -2021 2022 2023 2024 Draft en route cost-efficiency targets, expressed as determined en route unit cost (in real terms at 2017 prices) 169,6 PLN 174,8 PLN 320,1 PLN 200,2 PLN 172,0 PLN 163,2 PLN 39,85 EUR 41,07 EUR 75,24 EUR 47,05 EUR 40,42 EUR 38,35 EUR (33) Concerning the criterion laid down in point 1.4(a) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, the Commission observes that the en route DUC trend of Poland at charging zone level of -1,7 % per year over RP3 outperforms the Union-wide trend of +1,0 % over the same period. (34) Concerning the criterion laid down in point 1.4(b) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, the Commission observes that the long-term en route DUC trend of Poland at charging zone level over RP2 and RP3 of -0,4 % per year underperforms the long-term Union-wide trend of -1,3 % over the same period. (35) Concerning the criterion laid down in point 1.4(c) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, the Commission observes that the baseline value for the DUC of EUR 41,07 of Poland in real terms at 2017 prices (‘EUR2017’) is 5,4 % higher than the average baseline value of EUR 38,96 in EUR2017 of the relevant comparator group. However, the Commission notes that the determined en route unit cost of Poland for 2024 is lower by 6,7 % than the average of the comparator group. (36) The Commission has further examined whether the deviations observed in recitals 34 and 35 could be deemed necessary and proportionate under point 1.4(d) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, provided that the observed deviation from the long-term Union-wide DUC trend is exclusively due to additional determined costs related to measures necessary to achieve the performance targets in the key performance area of capacity or to restructuring measures within the meaning of Article 2(18) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. (37) In respect of the criterion specified under point 1.4(d)(i) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, the Commission notes that Poland sets out in its draft performance plan a wide range of measures undertaken by the air navigation service provider (PANSA) for the purpose of achieving the local capacity targets. Those measures are detailed and quantified in the draft performance plan. (38) Indeed, Poland plans a significant increase over RP3 in the number of air traffic controllers in operations at the Warsaw area control centre. Poland further explains that the training and recruitment of additional air traffic controllers will enable PANSA to implement airspace re-sectorisation as well as to accommodate forecasted traffic demand which is expected to reach 2019 levels by the end of RP3. (39) The Commission observes an increase in the investment costs related to capacity-enhancing projects such as upgrades and associated changes of the ATM system, the deployment of new operations rooms and radio communications stations, as well as the replacement and development of surveillance infrastructure. Poland points out that the planned RP3 capital expenditure is focused on capacity-related investments, and will enable airspace optimisation (e.g. three-layer vertical division of airspace) as well as enhanced resilience, scalability and flexibility of service provision. (40) Based on the detailed analysis by the performance review body, the Commission considers that the relevant measures outlined by Poland in the draft performance plan are indeed necessary to achieve the local capacity targets. Furthermore, having regard to the evaluation made by the performance review body, it can be concluded that the additional costs of those measures are larger than the deviation from the long-term Union-wide DUC trend referred to in recital 34. (41) In light of the considerations in recitals 37 to 40, the Commission therefore finds that the criterion set out in point 1.4(d)(i) is fulfilled in respect of Poland. (42) It follows from the foregoing observations that it is not necessary to further examine whether the criterion set out under point 1.4(d)(ii) would be fulfilled with regard to Poland. (43) On the basis of the findings set out in recitals 33 to 42, the proposed targets included in the draft performance plan of Poland should be assessed as consistent with the Union-wide performance targets in the key performance area of cost-efficiency. Review of draft cost-efficiency targets for terminal air navigation services (44) With regard to airports which fall within the scope of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317 as set out in Articles 1(3) and (4) of that Regulation, the Commission has complemented its assessment of draft en route cost-efficiency targets with the review of the draft cost-efficiency targets for terminal air navigation services in accordance with point 2.1(c) of Annex IV to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317. Those draft targets were found to raise concerns in respect of Poland. (45) Firstly, when comparing the RP3 terminal DUC trend with the en route DUC trend, the Commission has found that the terminal DUC trend of Poland’s terminal charging zone 1 of +2,2 % and charging zone 2 of +1,9 %, respectively, are higher than Poland’s en route DUC trend at charging zone level of -1,7 % over RP3. (46) Secondly, the Commission observes that the draft targets for the terminal DUC trend for Poland’s terminal charging zone 1 of +2,2 % over RP3 is higher than the actual terminal DUC trend of -8,9 % observed over RP2. In addition, the draft targets for the terminal DUC trend for Poland’s terminal charging zone 2 of +1,9 % over RP3 is higher than the actual terminal DUC trend of -2,6 % observed over RP2. (47) Therefore, the Commission considers, in connection with the adoption of its final performance plan in accordance with Article 16, point (a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317, that Poland should further justify the terminal cost-efficiency targets for RP3 in light of the observations set out in recitals 45 and 46, or should revise downwards those targets. CONCLUSIONS (48) On the basis of the assessment set out in recitals 9 to 47, the Commission has found that the performance targets contained in the draft performance plan submitted by Poland are consistent with the Union-wide performance targets. (49) The Commission notes that some Member States have indicated their intention to include cost items relating to airport drone detection in their RP3 cost bases. It has not been possible to precisely establish, based on the elements contained in the draft performance plans, to what extent Member States have included such determined costs in their RP3 cost bases and, where such costs have been included, to what extent they are incurred in relation to the provision of air navigation services and could thus be deemed eligible under the performance and charging scheme. The Commission services have sent an ad hoc information request to all Member States in order to gather relevant information, and will further examine the reported airport drone detection costs in the context of unit rate compliance verification. This Decision is without prejudice to the findings and conclusions of the Commission on the topic of drone detection costs. (50) In response to Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine, which started on 24 February 2022, the Union has adopted restrictive measures prohibiting Russian air carriers, any Russian-registered aircraft and any non-Russian-registered aircraft which is owned or chartered, or otherwise controlled by any Russian natural or legal person, entity or body from landing in, taking off from, or overflying the territory of the Union. Those measures are leading to a reduced air traffic in the airspace over the territory of the Union. The impact at the Union-wide level should however not be comparable to the reduction of air traffic which resulted from the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020. Therefore, it is appropriate to maintain the existing measures and processes for the implementation of the performance and charging scheme in RP3, HAS ADOPTED THIS DECISION: Article 1 The performance targets contained in the draft performance plan submitted by Poland, pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 549/2004, and listed in the Annex to this Decision, are consistent with the Union-wide performance targets for the third reference period set out in Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/891. Article 2 This Decision is addressed to the Republic of Poland. Done at Brussels, 13 April 2022. For the Commission Adina VĂLEAN Member of the Commission (1) OJ L 96, 31.3.2004, p. 1. (2) Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/317 of 11 February 2019 laying down a performance and charging scheme in the single European sky and repealing Implementing Regulations (EU) No 390/2013 and (EU) No 391/2013 (OJ L 56, 25.2.2019, p. 1). (3) Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2019/903 of 29 May 2019 setting the Union-wide performance targets for the air traffic management network for the third reference period starting on 1 January 2020 and ending on 31 December 2024 (OJ L 144, 3.6.2019, p. 49). (4) Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1627 of 3 November 2020 on exceptional measures for the third reference period (2020-2024) of the single European sky performance and charging scheme due to COVID-19 pandemic (OJ L 366, 4.11.2020, p. 7). ### EU Regulatory Context — FuelEU Maritime and RED II Alignment

FACT: The zero-emission requirement contains cross-references to EU frameworks: fuel sustainability and certification must be "aligned to FuelEU Maritime and the EU Renewable Energy Directive (RED)." *Source: Lloyd's Register Class News 03/2026, 5 February 2026. https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/class-news/03-26/

*Analytical inference:* As the EU develops implementing guidance under FuelEU Maritime — particularly on mass-balance chain-of-custody certification for biogas and on the GHG intensity calculation methodologies — that guidance will flow directly into the evidentiary basis for Norwegian fjord compliance. Changes to the EU voluntary certification schemes recognised under RED II will therefore affect the documentation the workspace must obtain from fuel suppliers.

*Operational implication:* The NMA consultation (2023) noted: "Whether or not these requirements should be part of the Environmental Safety Regulations depends on how the recast Renewable Energy Directive will be implemented in Norwegian legislation and whether it will apply to bunkering outside the European Economic Area (EEA) and to foreign ships during their stay in the EEA." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/ This remains an open implementation question.

**Re-check window:** MONITORING — Review when FuelEU Maritime implementing acts on biogas certification are published (expected 2025–2026 cycle); changes will directly alter Norwegian fjord documentation requirements.

### Shore Power — Flåm Facility

FACT: "The Parliament also decided that the state should ensure the establishment of shore power in Flåm, and the government will contribute with funds for this purpose." *Source: "Introducing Zero-Emission Requirements in the World Heritage Fjords," Ministry of Climate and Environment, 30 September 2024. https://www.regjeringen.no/en/whats-new/introducing-zero-emission-requirements-in-the-world-heritage-fjords/id3051481/

*Analytical inference:* Specific completion date and technical specifications for the Flåm shore-power installation are not stated in the primary sources. Once operational, the mandatory shore-power connection requirement will be triggered for vessels calling at Flåm — with direct consequences for port-call timing and power-supply logistics. **Re-check window:** MONITORING — Review when NMA or Norwegian Coastal Administration publish commissioning dates for Flåm shore power.

### IMO Strategy Trajectory

FACT: "In 2018, the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted a strategy on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions from ships. The IMO will adopt a new climate strategy in 2023 and the member States must decide on the requirements and mechanisms to ensure that the emissions targets are met. The ongoing EU and IMO work is expected to have an impact on the provisions that we propose in the regulatory amendments." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/ IMO's 2023 revised GHG strategy has since been adopted. *Analytical inference:* Further tightening of IMO targets may prompt NMA review of the 2032 transitional threshold for large vessels or the biogas eligibility conditions.

---

### Regulatory Obligation Placement

FACT: "The proposed requirements are aimed at the individual ship, but the company is responsible for ensuring that the requirements are complied with pursuant to section 4 of the Ship Safety and Security Act." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/

FACT: "Responsibility for compliance rests with the shipping company." *Source: Lloyd's Register Class News 03/2026, 5 February 2026. https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/class-news/03-26/

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether the workspace, in its role as freight forwarder coordinating bunkering, port-call logistics, or documentation for passenger vessel operators in the World Heritage fjords, carries any direct regulatory obligation under the Environmental Safety Regulations or the Ship Safety and Security Act requires counsel review. The primary compliance burden as defined falls on the ship and its operating company, not the freight forwarder; however, contractual liability and facilitation exposure depend on the specific services the workspace provides.

### Supply Chain Role in Practice

*Operational implication:* Workspaces that arrange fuel procurement for vessel operators are positioned as a critical upstream link in the compliance chain: the regulation's fuel-certification, biogas-separation, and one-month-bunkering-window requirements must be reflected in the specifications and documentation the workspace obtains from fuel suppliers and passes to vessel operators. A documentation failure at the bunkering stage surfaces directly on board the vessel during NMA enforcement.

*Operational implication:* Workspaces coordinating shore-power logistics at fjord ports — including Flåm, where the Norwegian state has committed funding for shore-power facility establishment — should treat shore-power connection compatibility as a standing specification item in port-call coordination, since non-connection where compatible infrastructure is available exposes the vessel operator to enforcement action.

---

### ACTION REQUIRED — Verify bunkering documentation chain for fjord-calling passenger vessels

Verify that any passenger vessel operator for whom the workspace arranges bunkering in or proximate to the World Heritage fjords has documentation on board confirming the fuel type meets the zero-emission definition. *Operational implication:* Under the adopted regulation, ships must carry onboard documentation demonstrating compliance with sustainability and GHG reduction criteria, proper certification of fuels in accordance with EU-recognised voluntary or national schemes, and supporting bunker delivery notes. *Source: Lloyd's Register Class News 03/2026, 5 February 2026. https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/class-news/03-26/

*Operational implication:* Workspaces arranging biogas bunkering for clients operating vessels of 10,000 GT and above must confirm the biogas was bunkered within one month prior to fjord entry and that the quantity matches expected energy demand during the fjord voyage — mass-balance gas-grid certificates are not accepted. *Source: NMA news release, 15 April 2025. https://www.sdir.no/en/news/zero-emission-requirement-for-the-world-heritage-fjords-adopted/

### ACTION REQUIRED — Assess shore-power connection compatibility for vessels at fjord ports

Assess whether vessels for which the workspace arranges port-call logistics are equipped with shore-power connections compatible with available fjord-port infrastructure. *Operational implication:* The regulation mandates that shipping companies must ensure their ships connect to shore power systems whenever compatible facilities are available to minimise emissions when berthed. *Source: Lloyd's Register Class News 03/2026, 5 February 2026. https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/class-news/03-26/ Connection incompatibility is the explicit basis for a temporary exemption claim (see Section 12 below), making compatibility assessment strategically important.

### ACTION REQUIRED — Map client vessel GT classifications against the phased deadline schedule

Map all passenger vessel operators the workspace serves against the 10,000 GT threshold to confirm which vessels face the 2026 deadline and which face the 2032 deadline. *Operational implication:* The two-phase schedule means compliance obligations differ materially by vessel size, and forwarding logistics arrangements — particularly bunkering specifications — must reflect the applicable phase for each vessel.

### WINDOW CLOSING — Temporary exemption window for sub-10,000 GT vessels runs to 31 December 2029

FACT: "If granted, the exemption may be valid for up to two years at a time but cannot be extended beyond 31 December 2029." *Source: Lloyd's Register Class News 03/2026, 5 February 2026. https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/class-news/03-26/ Operators who missed the 1 January 2026 deadline and qualify for a temporary exemption must apply promptly through the NMA. Workspaces coordinating operations for such clients should flag this closing window.

**Penalty summary slot (required):** FACT: "Failure to comply [may result] in administrative measures or violation fines under the Ship Safety and Security Act." *Source: Lloyd's Register Class News 03/2026, 5 February 2026. https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/class-news/03-26/ FACT: "The NMA may supervise that the ship complies with the requirements of the provision and may, where necessary, take various administrative measures pursuant to the Ship Safety and Security Act chapter 8 or by means of violation fines pursuant to chapter 9." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/ Specific penalty quantum: *Specific penalty quantum not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.* Engage legal counsel to confirm exposure under chapters 8 and 9 of the Ship Safety and Security Act.

### Technology Readiness Assessment

FACT: "We believe that the technology is not sufficiently mature for large passenger ships to be able to operate with zero emissions in the World Heritage fjords by 2026." This was the NMA's 2023 assessment, and informed the two-phase implementation. The NMA prepared a technology report: "Zero emissions from ships in the World Heritage fjords by 2026 — Supplement for the knowledge base with regard to the state of technological development." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/

FACT: "Menon estimates that large cruise ships will not be capable of being operated with no emissions in the World Heritage fjords until 2040." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/

### Battery Operations Already Demonstrated

FACT: "In June 2022, the 15,800 gross ton Havila Castor set a new record operating for three hours entirely on batteries in Geirangerfjord." *Source: "Norway Sets Phased-in Dates for Zero Emission Shipping in Fjords," The Maritime Executive, 29 August 2024. https://maritime-executive.com/article/norway-sets-phased-in-dates-for-zero-emission-shipping-in-fjords

FACT: "Collected data from Clarkson 'World Fleet Register' shows that there are currently 15 cruise ships that are able to use biogas and that 27 more have been ordered, including Havila Voyages' two new ships." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/

### Socioeconomic Impact Research (Menon Economics)

FACT: "According to Menon, an absolute zero emissions requirement will cause higher emissions than the zero alternative if a pessimistic scenario is applied. In the optimistic estimate the emissions are lower than in the zero alternative with an estimated difference of around 750 tonnes of CO₂ in 2026." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/

FACT: "Menon has estimated that an absolute requirement for zero emissions would result in a total turnover decrease of approximately NOK 234 million for Geiranger and Flåm. This means that the economic growth will decrease by around NOK 109 million and 184 jobs will be lost compared to the zero emissions alternative." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/

*Operational implication:* The Menon research finding that cruise traffic would relocate to other Norwegian fjords rather than invest in zero-emission technology — and that the number of port calls in Geiranger and Flåm would fall significantly — represents a material route-economics signal. Workspaces whose logistics networks include west-coast Norwegian fjord ports should track actual call-volume data, as the regulation may redirect traffic (and logistics demand) toward non-World Heritage fjord alternatives.

**GHG reduction qualification for hydrogen and ammonia:** FACT: Ships using hydrogen or ammonia must meet "the technical screening criteria for greenhouse gas reduction for the production of hydrogen and hydrogen-based fuels set out in Section 3.10 of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139 Annex I." ### Bunkering Specification and Timing Controls

**Scope:** All passenger vessel operators for whom the workspace arranges fuel procurement in or proximate to the World Heritage fjords.

**Deadline:** In force since 1 January 2026 for sub-10,000 GT vessels; 1 January 2032 for larger vessels.

**Gap from current operational baseline:** *Operational implication:* Standard fossil-fuel bunkering arrangements do not satisfy the regulation. Any workspace that previously arranged LNG, HFO, or MGO bunkering for fjord-calling passenger vessels must now source qualifying zero-emission fuels or certified biogas, with the 30-day pre-entry bunkering window and physical separation requirements built into the procurement schedule. The mass-balance grid-certificate pathway — common in European gas bunkering markets — is explicitly excluded for Norwegian fjord compliance.

**Required system change:** Build a bunkering compliance checklist for each fjord-calling vessel: (a) fuel type verification, (b) GHG reduction certification, (c) feedstock compliance, (d) physical separation confirmation, (e) 30-day bunkering window tracking, (f) quantity-match against expected fjord voyage energy demand, and (g) bunker delivery note alignment with on-board documentation.

### Shore-Power Compatibility Registry

**Scope:** All passenger vessels for which the workspace arranges port calls at fjord ports where shore power may be available.

**Required system change:** Maintain a vessel-port compatibility matrix documenting: (a) vessel shore-power connection standard, (b) available shore-power specification at each fjord port, and (c) outcome (compatible = mandatory connection; incompatible = obligation not triggered; infrastructure not yet available = obligation not yet triggered).

*Operational implication:* As Flåm shore-power infrastructure is commissioned with Norwegian state funding, vessels previously not subject to the connection obligation at Flåm will become subject to it. The workspace's port-call coordination must be updated when commissioning dates are announced.

**Required system change:** Negotiate with fuel suppliers (particularly biogas suppliers) to include: (a) certification of feedstock origin against Product Regulations Annex V Part A; (b) GHG reduction attestation consistent with RED II voluntary certification schemes; (c) confirmation of physical separation from fossil fuels throughout the supply chain; and (d) documentation delivery obligations for on-board records.

**Required system change:** Establish a standing notification protocol for passenger vessel operator clients: when a vessel is scheduled for a fjord call, trigger a pre-voyage compliance check covering fuel type, documentation, and shore-power compatibility no later than 35 days before scheduled entry (to allow the 30-day bunkering window to be met).

We do, however, require the use of the best available technology to reduce nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions." *Source: NMA Consultation, 7 April 2023. https://www.sdir.no/en/regelverk/hearings/consultation---proposed-implementation-of-zero-emissions-requirement-in-the-world-heritage-fjords-by-2026/

**Q: Does biogas sourced from the gas grid via mass-balance certification qualify?**
FACT: "Biogas sourced from the gas grid, accompanied by a certificate based on a mass balance system, does not meet the requirements for operating in the World Heritage fjords." *Source: NMA news release, 15 April 2025. https://www.sdir.no/en/news/zero-emission-requirement-for-the-world-heritage-fjords-adopted/

**Q: Does the regulation require measurement of actual ship emissions?**
FACT: "The regulation does not require verification of actual ship emissions." *Source: Lloyd's Register Class News 03/2026, 5 February 2026. https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/class-news/03-26/

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether the workspace, as freight forwarder, is an "obligated party" under the Ship Safety and Security Act in its capacity arranging fuel or port services for passenger vessel operators.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether liquid biofuels qualify as a compliant energy source under the enacted text, given Lloyd's Register's explicit statement that "the use of liquid biofuels is unclear." *Source: Lloyd's Register Class News 03/2026, 5 February 2026. https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/class-news/03-26/

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether the county ferry exemption ("the county's ferry will temporarily be exempt from the zero-emission requirement") applies to specific ferry routes the workspace's clients operate, and the duration and conditions of that exemption. *Source: "Introducing Zero-Emission Requirements in the World Heritage Fjords," Ministry of Climate and Environment, 30 September 2024. https://www.regjeringen.no/en/whats-new/introducing-zero-emission-requirements-in-the-world-heritage-fjords/id3051481/

pool.text: EQS: 5675 Circular - Series R Number: RSR 04-2025 Date: 14.04.2025 Case number: 2024/72534 Adoption of zero-emission requirements for cruise ships, tourist boats and ferries in the World Heritage fjords Introduction The Norwegian Government has decided to introduce zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords, effective from 1 January 2026 for passenger ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage, and from 1 January 2032 for passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards. Additionally, the Government has determined that passenger ships may use biogas as an alternative fuel, and that the use of shore power will be mandatory where such facilities are available. As a result of the Government's decision, the Norwegian Maritime Authority (NMA) has been mandated by the Ministry of Climate and Environment to establish zero-emission requirements for the World Heritage fjords. Accordingly, the NMA, on behalf of the Government, is introducing zero-emission requirements for cruise ships, tourist boats and ferries in the World Heritage fjords, as part of the Regulations of 30 May 2012 No. 488 on environmental safety for ships and mobile offshore units. History and consultative processes The adopted requirements are based on the follow-up of the Storting's petition resolution No. 672 of 3 May 2018, which mandates the introduction of zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords by 2026. They are also grounded in resolutions No. 690 and No. 691 of 25 February 2021, which request that the Government propose measures to ensure that the World Heritage fjords can continue to serve as ports of call beyond 2026. These measures include the establishment of shore power infrastructure in Flåm, supported by the State. In March 2022, the Ministry of Climate and Environment tasked the Norwegian Maritime Authority (NMA) with conducting a status review and submitting proposals on how to fulfil and implement the Storting’s petition resolution regarding the achievement of zero emissions from cruise ships, tourist boats and ferries in the World Heritage fjords as soon as technically feasible, and no later than 2026. The NMA submitted its proposal for zero-emission requirements for cruise ships, tourist boats and ferries in the World Heritage fjords to the Ministry of Climate and Environment on 2 January 2023. The proposal outlined a general rule mandating zero emissions, alongside a transitional arrangement permitting the use of biogas under specific conditions until the end of 2035. On 29 June 2023, the Ministry confirmed that the NMA’s proposal could proceed to public consultation. The proposal was circulated for review from 3 July to 3 October 2023, and also submitted for EEA consultation from July to October 2023. According to the NMA’s consultation letter, the proposed zero-emission requirement would regulate emissions of the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide and methane within the World Heritage fjords, and mandate the application of best available technology to reduce emissions of nitrous oxide. These amendments were intended to enter into force on 1 January 2026. More than 80 consultative statements were received during the consultation period. While all respondents supported the overarching objective of promoting greener shipping in the World Heritage fjords, the submissions revealed significant conflicts of interest. The statements reflected a range of 2 stakeholder perspectives and differing approaches to achieving the goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, encouraging continued maritime innovation and maintaining vessel traffic within the fjords. The consultation also revealed substantial disagreement regarding the technological maturity of zero- emission solutions for cruise ships, tourist boats and ferries. Following the consultation held from July to October 2023, the NMA developed a revised proposal and submitted its recommendation to the Ministry of Climate and Environment, presenting two alternatives, with the NMA recommending one of them. The recommendation was submitted to the Ministry on 13 December 2023. The NMA recommended an option that required zero emissions from passenger vessels starting in 2026, while allowing a transition arrangement until 2035, under which passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards could use biofuel, biogas, renewable fuels of non-biological origin or fuels produced from recycled carbon, as defined in Directive (EU) 2018/2001, as an alternative to the zero-emission requirement. Furthermore, the quantity of fuel used would need to correspond to the vessel’s actual energy consumption while operating in the World Heritage fjords. An important contextual basis for the NMA’s proposal was the EU’s climate package “Fit for 55”. The proposed regulatory framework for zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords was developed in alignment with the “Fit for 55” package, which aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 55% by 2030. Several elements of the EU’s climate package are relevant to the maritime sector, including the FuelEU Maritime Regulation, which seeks to increase demand for alternative fuels, and amendments to the Renewable Energy Directive, which establish sustainability criteria and greenhouse gas reduction requirements for alternative fuels. In developing the proposal for zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords, the NMA therefore aligned the specific requirements with the relevant EU legislation. On 5 September 2024, the NMA received a new assignment from the Ministry of Climate and Environment, as a follow-up to the 2023 tasks. This new mandate instructed the NMA to establish zero- emission requirements for cruise ships, tourist boats, and ferries in the World Heritage fjords, including detailed guidelines on the structure of the regulatory framework. The deadline for completion was set for 15 November 2025. Subsequently, on 17 December 2024, the NMA received a clarification of the 5 September 2024 assignment, extending the deadline to 31 January 2025. It was also requested that the Norwegian Environment Agency participate in the development of requirements related to sustainability, greenhouse gas reduction and documentation. Legal basis for the zero-emission requirement In the assignment dated 24 March 2022, the Norwegian Maritime Authority was instructed to establish regulatory provisions pursuant to chapter 5 of the Ship Safety and Security Act, relating to environmental safety. The legal basis for the adopted provisions is found in chapter 5, specifically sections 31 to 33 of the Ship Safety and Security Act, in conjunction with the Regulations of 30 May 2012 No. 488 on environmental safety for ships and mobile offshore units (Environmental Safety Regulations). The zero-emission requirements are set out in a new section 10b of the Environmental Safety Regulations. Thematically, this provision is intended to be positioned alongside other provisions addressing air pollution from ships. The World Heritage fjords are already defined in the preceding provision, section 10a third paragraph of the Regulations. Although the requirements apply to individual ships, it is the company's responsibility to ensure compliance in accordance with section 4 of the Ship Safety and Security Act. 3 The NMA may supervise compliance with the provision and, where necessary, implement administrative measures in accordance with chapter 8 of the Ship Safety and Security Act or impose violation fines pursuant to chapter 9. Limitation of scope In both previous work and under the current mandate, the scope of the term "cruise ships, tourist boats and ferries" has been limited to passenger ships. The term “passenger ship” is further defined in Chapter I, Part A, Regulation 2(f) of the SOLAS Convention and in section 2p of the Regulations on surveys, construction and equipment passenger ships engaged on domestic voyages. A passenger ship is defined as a vessel that may carry more than 12 passengers. It is further specified that high-speed passenger vessels also fall within this definition. On the zero-emission requirement In general terms, a zero-emission requirement entails the use of energy sources that do not produce direct emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) or methane (CH4). At an early stage in this process, the NMA established two definitions of zero emissions, which were presented in the consultation letter and draft Regulations circulated on 3 July 2023. The definitions used by the NMA are not reproduced here, but may be found in the NMA's consultation letter of July 2023 and the recommendation letter of December 20231. Under the mandate for establishing a zero-emission requirement in the World Heritage fjords, “zero emissions” are defined as follows: “The term zero emissions means that energy sources used must not result in direct emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) or methane (CH4). Fuels that generate direct emissions of greenhouse gases may be used to the extent necessary to ignite the energy sources. If nitrous oxide (N2O) is generated through the use of energy sources that meet the zero-emission requirement, the vessel shall use the best available technology to reduce such emissions.” Further details on the regulatory framework The Norwegian Maritime Authority, acting on behalf of the Ministry of Climate and Environment, has adopted regulatory amendments introducing a zero-emission requirement in the World Heritage fjords. This requirement will apply from 2026 to passenger ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage, and from 2032 to passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards. The provision allows the use of biogas as an alternative means of complying with the zero-emission requirement, including beyond 2032. In addition, the use of shore power is mandatory where such infrastructure is available. The content and wording of the regulatory provision on zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords stem from a political decision by the Government, and the rationale for the requirements follows from that decision. The zero-emission requirement is formulated in a technology-neutral manner, with no specific prescriptions as to how it must be met. It is therefore the responsibility of operators in the World Heritage fjords to use energy sources that do not result in direct emissions of carbon dioxide (CO₂) or methane (CH₄). However, where such energy sources are used, there are requirements for greenhouse gas emission reductions in accordance with the EU regulatory framework. Comments on the provisions Section 10b Special rules on emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) from passenger ships in the World Heritage fjords 1 Case number: 2023/75253 4 Section 10b first and second paragraphs The first paragraph of the provision stipulates that, from 1 January 2026, passenger ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage operating in the World Heritage fjords shall use energy sources that do not result in direct emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) or methane (CH4). According to the second paragraph, from 1 January 2032, passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards operating in the World Heritage fjords shall use energy sources that do not result in direct emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) or methane (CH4). Reference is made to the previously described definition of zero emissions. The term “passenger ship” is used in the provision. “Passenger ships” refers to vessels that may carry more than 12 passengers. Relevant ship types include cruise ships, ferries, high-speed craft and other tourist vessels. The term “World Heritage fjords” is already defined in section 10a third paragraph of the Environmental Safety Regulations. The zero-emission requirement set out in section 10b applies to all passenger ships while they are within the World Heritage fjords, regardless of whether they operate exclusively within the fjords or only partially transit through them. Section 10b third paragraph The third paragraph permits the use of fuels that are necessary to ignite the energy sources referred to in the first and second paragraphs. This provision is intended to allow the use of so-called “pilot fuels”. For example, when ammonia is used in combustion engines, small quantities of fuel, such as diesel, may be required to initiate combustion. Accordingly, the use of hydrogen and ammonia in combustion engines is not excluded as a means of complying with the zero-emission requirements set out in the first and second paragraphs. Section 10b fourth paragraph The fourth paragraph permits limited emissions of nitrous oxide (N₂O) resulting from the use of the energy sources specified in the first and second paragraphs. Combustion of ammonia and hydrogen may result in the formation of small quantities of nitrous oxide. To address this, the provision requires that such emissions be reduced through the use of best available technology. The NMA anticipates that, in parallel with the development of combustion engines for new fuels, catalytic technologies for maritime applications will also be developed to reduce nitrous oxide emissions. It is further expected that, over time, an international regulatory framework will be established to define acceptable levels of nitrous oxide emissions from combustion engines. Once such a framework is in place, the fourth paragraph may be revised to incorporate more detailed regulation of these specific emissions. Section 10b fifth paragraph The fifth paragraph sets out specific criteria for energy sources used to comply with the requirements of the first and second paragraphs of the provision. The first sentence establishes requirements where the energy source is a renewable fuel of non-biological origin, as defined in Article 2 second paragraph point 36 of the RED II Directive2. In such cases, the energy source must meet the greenhouse gas reduction criteria set out in Article 25(2) of the Directive. This means that the fuel must achieve a minimum 70% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, calculated in accordance with the methodology laid down in Regulation (EU) 2023/11853. By referring to the RED II framework for renewable fuels of non-biological origin, this also entails the use of methodologies to 2Directive (EU) 2018/2001 of 11 December 2018 on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources (recast) (RED II), as last amended by Regulation (EU) 2022/759. 3 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/1185 of 10 February 2023 supplementing Directive (EU) 2018/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council by establishing a minimum threshold for greenhouse gas emissions savings of recycled carbon fuels and by specifying a methodology for assessing greenhouse gas emissions savings from renewable liquid and gaseous transport fuels of non-biological origin and from recycled carbon fuels. 5 verify that the electricity used in the production process qualifies as renewable. In line with the approach taken in Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (FuelEU Maritime), section 10 b fifth paragraph refers to RED II, rather than RED III4. The second sentence provides that, where another type of fuel is used to comply with the first or second paragraph, the fuel must be certified in accordance with Article 10(2) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (FuelEU Maritime). An example of such a fuel is blue hydrogen, which, under the Fourth Gas Market Directive5, must achieve a minimum 70% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions to qualify. Section 10b sixth paragraph The Government has decided that all passenger ships may use biogas as an energy source, as an alternative to meeting the zero-emission requirements set out in the first and second paragraphs of section 10b. The use of biogas as an alternative energy source will also be permitted beyond 2032. For the use of biogas, specific sustainability and greenhouse gas reduction criteria must be met, in accordance with Article 29 of the RED II Directive and Article 10(1)(a) of the FuelEU Maritime Regulation. These criteria include a required reduction in GHG emissions of between 50% and 65%6 compared to a fossil fuel reference value. Additionally, the biogas must not be produced from food or feed crops, as defined in Article 2 paragraph 2 point 40 of the RED II Directive. The sixth paragraph also sets out requirements regarding the timing and method of biogas bunkering in order to satisfy the conditions for calling at the World Heritage fjords. Biogas must be bunkered within the final month before the ship enters the World Heritage fjords, and the amount bunkered must correspond to the amount expected to be used during the voyage though the fjords. In addition, the biogas must be kept separate from fossil fuels until it is bunkered on board the ship. It is not considered practical for vessels to operate exclusively on pure biogas while sailing in the World Heritage fjords. Accordingly, there is no requirement for the biogas to be stored in dedicated onboard tanks. Biogas sourced from the gas grid, accompanied by a certificate based on a mass balance system, does not meet the requirements for operating in the World Heritage fjords. Section 10b seventh paragraph According to the seventh paragraph of the provision, passenger ships operating in the World Heritage fjords are required to use shore power where such facilities are available. The facilitation and provision of sufficient shore power capacity is considered an important measure for achieving zero emissions in these fjords. Using shore power while ships are at berth could be an effective way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from passenger ships in the World Heritage fjords. To ensure that established shore power facilities are used and thereby contribute to emissions reductions, it is considered appropriate to impose a requirement for ships to connect to shore power whenever such facilities are available. The phrase "available to the ships" is understood to mean that the shore power connection points on both the ship and the port are compatible, and that the port can supply the ship with the required shore power. Section 10b eighth paragraph 4 RED III refers to Directive (EU) 2018/2001 as amended by Directive (EU) 2023/2413, Directive (EU) 2024/1405 and Directive (EU) 2024/1711. The deadline for implementation of RED III in the EU is 25 May 2025, and at present, the FuelEU Regulation formally refers to RED II. 5 Directive (EU) 2024/1788 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 on common rules for the internal markets for renewable gas, natural gas and hydrogen, amending Directive (EU) 2023/1791 and repealing Directive 2009/73/EC (recast). 6 The required level of greenhouse gas reduction depends on the date on which the production facility began producing the biofuel. 6 The eighth paragraph requires that ships carry documentation on board confirming compliance with the fuel-related requirements set out in this provision. Regarding the demonstration of compliance with sustainability criteria and greenhouse gas reduction requirements for fuel, such compliance must be substantiated through certification and supporting documentation in accordance with Article 10(3) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1805. This includes fuel delivery notes which, where relevant, must be supplemented with the information specified in Annex I of the Regulation. Additionally, the fuel must be certified under either EU-recognised voluntary schemes or approved national schemes. Should it be revealed that the vessel does not comply with the documentation requirements, this may form the basis for administrative sanctions under chapter 8 of the Ship Safety and Security Act, or for the imposition of violation fines pursuant to chapter 9 of the Act. Section 10b ninth paragraph The Government has determined that there is a need for an exemption from the zero-emission requirements for passenger ships deployed in regular service due to planned roadworks or in response to emergency situations. The NMA assumes that this exemption also applies to ambulance services and school transport. Section 10b tenth paragraph The Government has decided that county-operated high-speed craft shall be exempt from the zero- emission requirements. In this context, “county-operated high-speed craft” refers to vessels operating under public service contracts. Other operators may run high-speed craft in the World Heritage fjords, but as long as these are not operating under a public service contract, they will not fall under the exemption. Section 10c Exemption for passenger ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage operating in World Heritage fjords This provision gives the Norwegian Maritime Authority (NMA) the option, but not the obligation, to grant exemptions, as indicated by the use of the word "may" in the first paragraph. The exemption is intended as a narrowly defined opportunity for small passenger ships that have operated in the World Heritage fjords and are unable to continue operations due to the zero-emission requirements and limited charging infrastructure. As specified in subparagraph a, the exemption applies to established vessels that were operating in the World Heritage fjords in 2024 and intend to continue operating there until 2030. The provision is designed to accommodate companies whose passenger ships operate exclusively within the World Heritage fjords and who, due to the zero-emission requirements, face a lack of viable alternatives stemming from limited infrastructure and insufficient access to electricity. It is not intended to apply to companies operating passenger ships on routes that include both the World Heritage fjords and other fjords. The requirement for continuous operation in the World Heritage fjords in 2024 up to the time of application is crucial. The exemption is aimed at ships already established in the area and is not intended for new market entrants. Any new operations must comply with the zero-emission requirements as of 1 January 2026. Furthermore, as set out in subparagraph c, the company must demonstrate that compliance with the zero-emission requirement in section 10b is not feasible due to an inability to obtain approval for access to shore power. To satisfy this condition, the company must provide documentation showing that access to shore power is not currently available, along with a plan outlining how it intends to meet the zero- emission requirements. Subparagraph d further requires the company to document a concrete plan for gaining access to shore power. This condition has been deliberately formulated to allow for flexibility, recognising that there may be various legitimate ways for companies to demonstrate such planning. For this reason, the wording enables the NMA to conduct a holistic assessment of whether the company has provided adequate documentation. Part of this condition also involves proving that it is technically feasible for the specific 7 vessel to operate on batteries once shore power becomes available. Many of the small vessels currently operating in the World Heritage fjords are older vessels, which may pose challenges for retrofitting with battery solutions. In these cases, the company must demonstrate that it has a credible and technically viable plan for introducing battery solutions on board. Subparagraphs a and b set out relatively straightforward conditions that require the company to document objective facts. Subparagraphs c and d, however, involve a more discretionary assessment by the NMA. Accordingly, exemption decisions will be based on a concrete, overall evaluation of the adequacy of the company’s documentation concerning both the lack of shore power access and the ship’s future connection plans. The decisive elements in assessing applications for exemption under this provision will therefore be subparagraphs c and d, along with the level of documentation required for the NMA to consider these conditions satisfied. Exemptions may be granted for a maximum of two years at a time and, in any case, not beyond 31 December 2029. The wording "up to two years" does not imply an automatic two-year exemption; rather, the duration will be individually assessed in each case. These temporary exemptions are intended to encourage companies to comply with the zero-emission requirements as soon as possible. This goal must be balanced with the need for predictability for ship operators and the administrative burden associated with applying for exemptions. Accordingly, exemptions of up to two years may be granted. No exemption may extend beyond 31 December 2029, as the objective is for sufficient electricity infrastructure to be in place in the World Heritage fjords by that date. This means, for instance, that a ship applying for exemption on 1 June 2029 may only be granted a six-month exemption, valid until 31 December 2029. Section 14f first sentence The new provision on zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords will be covered by the exemption authority set out in section 14f of the Environmental Safety Regulations. This means that ships protected or preserved by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage will also be eligible to apply for an exemption from the zero-emission requirements applicable in the World Heritage fjords. Administrative and financial implications The zero-emission requirements for passenger ships operating in the World Heritage fjords, which will enter into force in 2026 and 2032 respectively, will have implications for companies, local communities and public authorities. As part of the preparatory work, Menon conducted a socio-economic analysis on behalf of the NMA, which, among other things, examined the financial impacts of introducing zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords. The report was published in October 2022. For the current assessment of administrative and financial implications, relevant parts of this report have been used, along with input from affected stakeholders outlining the anticipated consequences of the adopted requirements. Consequences for the industry Several stakeholders have indicated that implementing the established zero-emission requirements will be challenging. In general, batteries represent a viable option for ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage, and access to charging infrastructure will be a critical prerequisite for meeting the core zero-emission requirement. Technologies based on hydrogen and ammonia are under development; however, at present, these fuels are not practically available as alternatives to conventional fuels for small passenger vessels. 8 With regard to alternative fuels, operators of the smallest passenger ships have noted that biogas is not a viable option, as it is incompatible with diesel engines. The introduction of zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords is therefore expected to have significant impacts on vessels of less than 10,000 gross tonnage. Given that many stakeholders have stated that it will be difficult, or nearly impossible, to meet the established requirements, the exemption mechanism set out in section 10c is expected to be especially valuable for some industry actors. This exemption may enable continued operations, provided the vessels in question satisfy the conditions set out in the provision. For passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards, the zero-emission requirement does not enter into force until 1 January 2032. These ships may therefore continue operating as normal until that date and have several years to adapt to the new requirements. Nevertheless, many cruise companies have reported that they anticipate significant challenges in complying with the regulations once they take effect. It was also noted that biogas producers in Europe currently supply biogas only via the common European gas grid, delivered to customers with guarantees of origin or certificates in accordance with the EU regulatory framework. It was also noted that biogas producers in Europe currently supply biogas only via the common European gas grid, delivered to customers with guarantees of origin or certificates in accordance with the EU regulatory framework. The requirement for physical separation diverges from the certification method permitted under the Renewable Energy Directive. Industry representatives have particularly emphasised that this requirement is both highly impractical and costly. The requirement for physical separation of biogas up to the point of bunkering is part of the mandate related to the establishment of zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords. As physically separated biogas is not readily available, this requirement is likely to render biogas an impractical fuel option for passenger ships operating in these fjords, even though several larger cruise ships are equipped with engines capable of running on biogas. Since the zero-emission requirements for ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards will not take effect until 2032, there is time for further technological development and adaptation within the industry. Financial implications for local communities in the World Heritage fjords The 2022 Menon report indicated that, overall, the introduction of zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords would lead to reduced income. Local communities in these areas are heavily reliant on tourism from the cruise industry. Since the requirements for larger ships will not take effect until 2032, it is expected that there will be minimal change before that time. Cruise ships will continue to operate in the fjords, thereby generating income for local businesses and ports. However, it remains difficult to predict how the situation will evolve once the new requirements enter into force in 2032. From 1 January 2025, stricter rules on NOx emissions have come into effect, requiring all passenger ships of more than 1,000 gross tonnage to comply with the NOx Tier III standard, pursuant to section 14c of the Environmental Safety Regulations and MARPOL Regulation VI/13. These rules restrict cruise traffic in the World Heritage fjords with respect to NOx emissions, permitting only vessels that meet the Tier III standard to operate in the area. As a result, some reduction in cruise traffic is expected. Consequences for the Norwegian Maritime Authority The NMA will be responsible for overseeing the implementation and enforcement of the new requirements in the World Heritage fjords, which will also necessitate training for surveyors. Furthermore, a significant amount of time will be required to inform the industry and respond to enquiries and requests for clarification regarding the new requirements. The exemption provision is expected to increase the administrative workload for the NMA. The provision has been deliberately formulated to be narrow in scope, and the conditions are intended to limit the 9 number of eligible passenger ships. Nevertheless, several of the criteria – particularly subparagraphs c and d, which involve discretionary evaluations – may make the processing of exemption applications time-consuming. That said, it is reasonable to assume that only a limited number of ships will qualify for exemption. However, considerable administrative effort will still be required to assess whether applicants meet the necessary conditions. It is anticipated that several companies may consider themselves eligible and submit applications, even in cases where – based on the authorities’ assessment –they do not fulfil the required criteria.
